'''Léon Charles Prudent Van Hove''' (10 February 1924 – 2 September 1990)<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://wiki.arts.kuleuven.be/wiki_nl/index.php?title=Van_Hove,_L%C3%A9on_Charles_Prudent_%281924-1990%29&setlang=nl|title = Van Hove, Léon Charles Prudent (1924–1990)|accessdate = 2 September 2015|website = Bestor – Belgian Science and Technology Online Resources|publisher = KU Leuven}}</ref> was a [[Belgium|Belgian]] [[physicist]] and a Director General of [[CERN]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Léon Van Hove 1924–1990|journal=CERN Courier|date=September 1990|volume=30|issue=7|page=7|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1731815}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Martin|first1=André|last2=Levaux|first2=Paul|last3=Gabathuler|first3=E.|last4=Woltjer|first4=L.|last5=Hugenholtz|first5=N.M.|authorlink5=Nicolaas Marinus Hugenholtz|title=Léon Van Hove 1924–1990|journal=CERN Courier|date=March 1991|volume=31|issue=2|pages=20–27|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1731889}}</ref> He developed a scientific career spanning [[mathematics]], [[solid state physics]], [[Particle physics|elementary particle]] and [[nuclear physics]] to [[cosmology]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Jacob, Maurice|title=Obituary: Léon Van Hove|journal=Physics Today|date=May 1991|volume=44|issue=5|pages=78|url=http://www.physicstoday.org/resource/1/phtoad/v44/i5/p78_s1?bypassSSO=1|doi=10.1063/1.2810123|bibcode=1991PhT....44e..78J|access-date=3 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005014820/http://www.physicstoday.org/resource/1/phtoad/v44/i5/p78_s1?bypassSSO=1|archive-date=5 October 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Biography==
Van Hove studied mathematics and physics at the [[Université libre de Bruxelles]] (ULB). In 1946 he received his PhD in mathematics at the ULB. From 1949 to 1954 he worked at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] by virtue of his meeting with [[Robert Oppenheimer]]. Later he worked at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] and was a professor and Director of the Theoretical Physics Institute at the [[University of Utrecht]] in [[the Netherlands]]. In the 1950s he laid the theoretical foundations for the analysis of [[inelastic neutron scattering]] in terms of the [[dynamic structure factor]]. In 1958, he was awarded the [[Francqui Prize]] in Exact Sciences. In 1959, he received an invitation to become the head of the Theory Division at CERN in [[Geneva]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Who's who in Cern: Léon van Hove: Director, Theoretical Studies division|journal=CERN Courier|date=August 1960|volume=1|issue=13–14|page=2|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1728432}}</ref> In 1975 Prof. Van Hove was appointed [[List of Directors General of CERN|CERN Director-General]], with [[John Adams (Physicist)|John Adams]], responsible for the research activities of the Organization.<ref>{{Cite web|url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/25555|title = Appointment of the Directors-General of the Organization| date=1975 |accessdate = 2 September 2015|publisher = CERN}}</ref> The [[LEP|LEP project]] was proposed during Van Hove's tenure as Director General.<ref>{{Cite web|url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/27910|title = The LEP Project, Phase 1 – Proposal of the Directors-General to the CERN Council| date=1980 |accessdate = 2 September 2015|publisher = CERN}}</ref>

==Controversies==
In 1963–64, [[George Zweig]] developed a particle physics model in which [[hadrons]] comprise fundamental constituents called "aces," independently of [[Murray Gell-Mann]]'s [[quark]] model. As head of CERN's Theory Division, Van Hove opposed the work, reportedly refusing permission for journal submission, instructing staff not to type the manuscript, and cancelling a seminar where Zweig planned to present it.<ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with George Zweig |url=https://ep-news.web.cern.ch/content/interview-george-zweig |website=CERN EP News |publisher=European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) |date=2013-10-24 |access-date=2026-07-28 }}</ref> Zweig instead circulated the work as CERN preprints, which became influential despite not being formally published. Van Hove's actions substantially reduced the visibility of Zweig's work at a critical moment and are widely regarded as having contributed to Zweig's failure to receive the recognition that ultimately culminated in Gell-Mann alone receiving the 1969 Nobel Prize.<ref>{{cite web |last=Dorigo |first=Tommaso |title=George Zweig's Brilliant Intuition, And Van Hove's Horrible Censorship |url=https://science20.com/a_quantum_diaries_survivor/george_zweigs_brilliant_intuition_and_van_hoves_horrible_censorship-144522 |website=Science 2.0 |date=2014-11-18 |access-date=2026-07-28 }}</ref> Van Hove cited publication policy, though scientific skepticism toward fractionally charged constituents likely also played a role.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Llewellyn Smith |first=Chris |title=From concrete quarks to QCD: a personal perspective |journal=The European Physical Journal H |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=13 |year=2023 |doi=10.1140/epjh/s13129-023-00061-4 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjh/s13129-023-00061-4 |access-date=2026-07-28 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Today, both Zweig and Gell-Mann are recognized as independent originators of the quark model.

==Awards==
* [[Francqui Prize]], 1958
* [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]], 1962
* Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], 1964<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leon Charles Prudent Van Hove |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/leon-charles-prudent-van-hove |access-date=2022-06-21 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Max Planck Medal]], 1974
* Member, United States [[National Academy of Sciences]], 1980<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leon Van Hove |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/leon-van-hove-9no9hw/ |access-date=2022-06-21 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>
* Member, [[American Philosophical Society]], 1980<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Leon+Van+Hove&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-06-21 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>
There is a square, Square Van Hove, named after Van Hove at [[CERN]], [[Geneva]], Switzerland.
